title: The sharp tongue
hook: Kabir mocked empty ritual at the mosque, at the temple, and in his own prayer beads
tomorrow: she tied a knot for each insult. why did her cloths weigh the same?

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the granth: a weaver's songs set beside the Gurus' own and bowed to as Guru. Today, the last day with Kabir, and he isn't polite.

The church is full, Hannah is walking down the aisle, and Theo's cousin leans over during the opening prayer to mutter a joke about the God stuff. Zoe almost laughs. Kabir would have had something to say, and he'd have said it to everyone in the room. Now go back to his own city. Kabir stops under a mosque as the call to prayer rings out from the top. You piled up pebbles and stones to build this, he says, and the mullah climbs up and shouts. Has God gone deaf?
screen: `A JOKE DURING THE PRAYER.` → `UNDER THE MOSQUE.` → `HAS GOD GONE DEAF?`

segments.voice: Then he turns to worship before images of stone. If God is found by worshiping a stone, he says, I'll worship a whole mountain. Better the grinding stone at home: the world eats the flour it grinds. And then he turns on his own practice. Kabir's own path is remembering God's name, and many who remember it count on a mala, a string of beads. The beads turn in the hand, he says, the tongue turns in the mouth, and the mind wanders off in every direction. That isn't remembering. So who did Kabir mock hardest? Whoever was going through the motions, and that included people doing exactly what he taught. Here's the teaching under the sharp tongue: for Kabir, the form isn't the worship. What counts is the heart turned toward God. A shout from a tower, a stone in a shrine, a bead in his own hand can all carry that, or all be empty. His target in these couplets is the motion without the heart. He mocked the empty. Which brings it back to the pew. Kabir would have aimed at the cousin's joke too: a sneer on autopilot is its own empty ritual. And three rows up, Theo stood and read his sister's passage, meaning every word.
screen: `A STONE, OR A MOUNTAIN?` · `THE BEADS TURN; THE MIND WANDERS.` · `THE FORM ISN'T THE WORSHIP.` · `A SNEER CAN BE EMPTY TOO.` · then, large: `MOCKING THE EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Pick one small thing you say or do every day without thinking: a thank you, a grace before eating, a goodnight. Do it now, once, slowly, meaning every word. Then sit with the difference between the motion and the meaning.
The sharp tongue: Kabir's mockery of empty ritual in every camp, his own included, aimed at the motion without the heart.
Keep this one: mocking the empty, never the one who means it. Eight days, and the weaver's song is done.

howItsDone: Kabir's sharp dohas against empty ritual are sung in bhajan gatherings and quoted as a check on one's own practice; in the Kabir Panth, remembering the name inwardly is valued above outward forms.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3: written new in recipe v3, shape story (Kabir walking his city: mosque, shrine, his own beads). Teaching named: for Kabir the heart turned toward God is the worship, not the form; he mocked the empty, his own practice included. The hook answers day 1519's question.

Sensitivity: the mosque and shrine couplets are Kabir's own, quoted in paraphrase as his; the lesson balances them with his couplet against his own bead practice and says he never mocked people who meant it. A Keeper from Islam and from Hinduism should read the tone.
Check the transliterations of the three dohas; paraphrased only. 'Now go back to his own city' sets the scene; the dohas themselves don't place him at a particular mosque.
